summary.one_line: A Kolkata family-run imitation-jewellery wholesaler (City Girl / Manikya brands, about 82% wholesale, about 66% West Bengal) raising Rs 34.99 crore, all fresh issue, on NSE SME to move into in-house plating and B2C showrooms. Profits tripled in FY26 but operating cash flow was negative, inventory days tripled, the expansion has no orders placed and approvals are still pending, and there is no visible moat.
bull_points: The whole Rs 34.99 crore is a fresh issue with no offer for sale, so all the money goes to the company; promoters go from 99.67% to 72.26% and do not cash out at the IPO (S1, S3).

Reported growth is strong: revenue from operations went from Rs 13.28 crore (FY24) to Rs 17.77 crore (FY25) to Rs 30.36 crore (FY26), and PAT went from Rs 0.95 crore to Rs 2.00 crore to Rs 6.29 crore (S14, S17).
The balance sheet is lightly geared, with borrowings of Rs 1.70 crore at FY26 (debt/equity 0.11) and Rs 3.06 crore at June 2026 (S1).
Sales are spread across many small buyers: 12 distributors, about 550 dealers, about 800 retailers and about 120 shop-in-shop counters. The top 5 customers are only 11.11% of FY26 sales (S21, S14).
bear_points: FY26 operating cash flow was negative Rs 67.79 lakh even though operating profit before working-capital changes was Rs 7.34 crore. Inventory went from Rs 1.09 crore (FY24) to Rs 7.83 crore (FY26) (S18).
Inventory days went from 38 to 117 in two years, and the board's own projections take them to 144 and the working-capital cycle to 107 days (S19).
The plating-facility capex (Rs 8.80 crore) has no machinery orders signed, and its trade, factory, pollution and fire approvals are still pending. Handover is targeted for September 2027 (S20).
Concentration is high: Eastern India was 86.32% of FY26 revenue and West Bengal alone 65.77% (S8).

There is no visible moat. The company outsources manufacturing to non-exclusive karigars and contract makers, sells mostly undifferentiated wholesale product, and competes with many organised and unorganised players (S2, S27).
watch_points: Final-day subscription by category. As of the opening morning (5 Oct 2026) no subscription data had been published (S26).
Whether FY27 margins hold near FY26's level. FY24 operating EBITDA was only about Rs 0.11 crore, and FY26 still included Rs 1.18 crore of other income (S1, S17).
Progress on Baruipur plating-facility approvals and machinery orders, and on the Ezra Street showroom licences (S20).
Inventory and receivables in the H1 FY27 results, which will show whether the cash-flow mismatch is reversing (S18, S19).

reasoning: The use of proceeds is a strategic pivot, not an expansion of a proven model. About Rs 22.25 crore goes to an in-house PVD plating plant, two Kolkata showrooms and their opening inventory. The plant has no signed machinery agreements and none of its approvals yet, and the B2C showrooms take a wholesale-led business (82.53% wholesale) into retail, which it has little track record in (S20, S21).

Earnings are not yet backed by cash. FY26 PAT was Rs 6.29 crore, but operating cash flow was negative Rs 67.79 lakh, and FY24 operating cash flow was also negative. The board's own projections raise net working capital from Rs 7.48 crore to Rs 18.79 crore by FY28, mostly from internal accruals that have not been generating cash (S18, S19).

Profitability jumped very recently and depends partly on other income. FY24 EBITDA excluding other income was about Rs 0.11 crore against Rs 1.18 crore of other income, and the three-fold PAT jump came in the year straight before the IPO. One strong year is too short a record to trust a 20%+ PAT margin in a commoditised product (S1, S17).

There is no moat. Production is outsourced to non-exclusive karigars and contract makers (72.65% of revenue comes from contract-manufactured goods), plating is subcontracted in Mumbai, the brands are regional, and the market is crowded with funded online and offline brands such as Kushals, Rubans, Sukkhi and GIVA (S20, S21, S27).

Governance is thin. It is a single family: the father and three sons hold all four executive seats and 99.67% of the shares, and the three independent directors were all appointed in February 2026 just ahead of the IPO. Related-party transactions were 66.40% of revenue in FY24, there are no lease papers for the registered office, and a 16:1 bonus in March 2026 brought the promoters' average cost to Rs 0.37-0.65 per share (S22, S17, S24, S23).

The risk profile is lopsided for a Rs 2.62 lakh minimum ticket on an illiquid SME platform. Revenue is concentrated in Eastern India (86.32%), the expansion is still at the execution stage, and the lead manager's past listings have been mixed. Nothing here justifies taking that risk before the cash-flow and capex questions are answered (S8, S1, S28).

subsections.title: What the company does and how it earns revenue

blocks.text: R.K. Fashion Accessories was incorporated in March 2010 as Satabadi Distributor and renamed in 2011. It designs and sources 24-carat gold-plated and stone-studded imitation jewellery, has it made by contract manufacturers and local karigars (artisans), and distributes it mainly wholesale. It also trades branded cosmetics and earns rental and commission income from hotel properties (S2, S6). It launched its two brands in 2018: City Girl (regular-wear gold-look jewellery) and Manikya (CZ / American-diamond pieces). It started shop-in-shop (SIS) counters in 2021 and entered the hotel business in 2023 (S2, S9).

In FY26 revenue from operations was Rs 30.36 crore. Imitation jewellery made up 81.88% (Rs 24.86 crore), cosmetics 16.15% (Rs 4.90 crore) and rental/commission income 1.97% (Rs 59.73 lakh) (S21). The cosmetics line is pure trading and the hotel income is passive: from FY25 the hotels have been leased to third parties instead of being run directly (S12, S21). So in practice this is a jewellery distribution business with a small cosmetics trading arm attached.

blocks.caption: FY26 revenue mix (Rs crore, % of revenue from operations) (S21)

blocks.text: Within jewellery, regular-wear City Girl products made Rs 17.99 crore (72.38% of jewellery revenue) and wedding jewellery Rs 5.85 crore (23.54%). By product type, bangles (22.38%) and sets (20.67%) were the largest (S21). The share of contract-manufactured goods in revenue rose from 57.4% in FY24 to 72.6% in FY26 (S12). Pricing is catalogue-led wholesale selling across several price points; the filings summarised here give no average selling prices (S2).

The customer base is wide and made up of small buyers: 12 distributors, about 550 dealers, about 800 retailers, and about 120 SIS counters run under corporate partnerships with national retail chains (S21, S10). E-commerce is small. Online orders were roughly flat at 65,994 (FY24), 61,951 (FY25) and 63,665 (FY26), and online revenue was only Rs 1.47 crore in FY26 (S21). The 'over 10,000 monthly online orders' line in marketing material does not fit the roughly 5,300 a month implied by the FY26 order count (S10, S21).
Customer concentration is moderate. The top 5 customers were 11.11% of FY26 sales and the top 10 were 15.15% (S14, S2). The prospectus still lists dependence on key customers as a risk factor (S6).

Geographic concentration is the real issue. Eastern India (West Bengal, Odisha, Bihar, Jharkhand) was 86.32% of FY26 revenue, up from 76.04% in FY24, and West Bengal alone was 65.77% (S8). Sales outside Eastern India actually fell as a share, from 23.96% to 13.68%, so the business has become more regional, not less (S8).

The company designs in-house and outsources assembly to local karigars and third-party contract manufacturers, mostly in Kolkata (S6, S9). The karigars are non-exclusive and on short-term arrangements, so they can work for competitors or leave (S2, S10). Plating is currently subcontracted to Mumbai-based processors. Management cites the resulting transit delays as the reason for building its own plating plant (S20).

Supplier concentration is higher than customer concentration. The top 5 suppliers were 34.10% of FY26 raw-material purchases and the top 10 were 45.85% (S14, S2). By source, Maharashtra supplied 48.60% (Rs 7.98 crore) of raw materials and Gujarat 6.49%, and direct gold procurement made up 36.67% (Rs 6.02 crore) (S21). That gold exposure ties input costs to gold prices even though the product is imitation jewellery.

items: Premises: the registered office (Room A-201) and business place (Room A-107) are in Bagree Market, Kolkata, and neither has a rent agreement or rent receipt. The company says a 17 September 2018 fire destroyed the tenancy records and the owner cannot be traced (S24).

Owned assets include a 900 sq ft warehouse on Tarak Dutta Road and a 6,520 sq ft four-storey building at 161/6 Rash Behari Avenue. That building is the planned B2C showroom, and its ground floor has been operating since April 2026 (S24, S20).
There were 50 permanent employees as of June 2026, which is a lean team for about 1,400 trade accounts and 120 counters (S1, S21).
Quality claims in marketing material include a nine-stage inspection process and a six-month colour guarantee (S14).

blocks.text: Imitation, costume or fashion jewellery in India is a large and growing but fragmented category. Technavio (January 2025) expects the Indian costume-jewellery market to grow by USD 1.16 billion over 2025-2029, an 11.4% CAGR. It cites affordable pricing, millennial demand and e-commerce as drivers, and low durability as the main constraint (S27). Other research houses put the Indian artificial-jewellery market at roughly USD 5 billion in 2025, growing at about 9-10% a year (search-result summaries only; not independently verified) (S27).
Record gold prices are a real tailwind because they push wedding and occasion buyers toward imitation pieces (S27, S10). That tailwind lifts every player, though. It is not specific to RKFAL.
The industry section of the RHP could not be read directly (see method), so no RHP-commissioned market-share figure is available for RKFAL. None of the secondary sources reviewed quote one.

Organised competitors include funded D2C and omnichannel brands such as Kushals Fashion Jewellery, Rubans Accessories, Sukkhi Online, GIVA, YouBella, Isharya, Zariin and Nykaa Fashion (S27). Most are larger and more digitally native than RKFAL. Its main competition, though, is the many unorganised Kolkata, Mumbai and Rajkot wholesalers and karigar workshops selling into the same dealer networks. Reviewers describe the category as competitive and trend-sensitive (S10, S6).

There is no close listed comparable. The comparison sets on aggregator pages use unrelated companies (eyewear, apparel, watches, luggage), which itself shows how niche and small this business is (search-result summary) (S6).

No real moat is visible. There is no import-substitution angle, no technical or regulatory barrier, no market-share claim, and nothing the company is the only maker of. Manufacturing is outsourced to non-exclusive artisans (S2). Plating is outsourced. The brands are regional, with 86% of sales in the east (S8), and online traction has been flat for three years (S21).

What it does have are trade relationships built over about 15 years in Kolkata's Bagree Market wholesale cluster, a catalogue of designs, and SIS shelf space in retail chains (S21, S10). Those are useful working advantages, but competitors can copy them, and the prospectus's stated strengths ('management expertise', 'established reputation', 'quality focus') are generic (S7, S6).

Verdict on moat: none. The proposed in-house plating plant may improve turnaround and margins if it is executed well, but it would be a cost advantage that rivals can replicate, not a barrier to entry.

Restated figures show revenue from operations up 129% in two years and PAT up more than six-fold (S17, S14). Sources disagree on EBITDA because some include other income and some exclude it. The table shows both. Excluding other income, FY24 was barely above break-even at the operating level, and that year's profit came almost entirely from Rs 1.18 crore of other income (S1, S17).

The FY26 step-up is large. Revenue rose 71% (total income 77%) and PAT 215%, and operating EBITDA margin expanded from about 17% to about 24% (S13, S1). The Q1 FY27 PAT margin of 24.4% suggests the improvement has held into the first quarter (S1). Still, the history of high margins is only five quarters long, and FY26 PAT still includes Rs 1.18 crore of other income. The sources reviewed do not explain what that other income is (S17).

Profit jumped sharply in the year straight before the IPO. Investors should not extrapolate a 20%+ net margin in imitation jewellery wholesale, which is a low-barrier activity, without a longer record.

Leverage is low (debt/equity 0.11 at FY26, 0.17 at June 2026), but borrowings almost doubled in the June quarter, from Rs 1.70 crore to Rs 3.06 crore (S1). The bigger change is in working capital. Inventory days went 38 to 85 to 117 and receivable days 16 to 21 to 30, while payable days fell from 95 to 83. The cash cycle moved from negative 41 days to positive 64 days in two years (S19).

blocks.caption: Working-capital cycle, actual and board-approved projections (days) (S19)

blocks.text: Net worth also benefited from a March 2024 amalgamation that issued 5,27,516 shares. A 16-for-1 bonus in March 2026 then capitalised reserves, which is why reserves fall from Rs 9.16 crore to Rs 4.91 crore in FY26 while net worth rises (S23, S1).

This is the main financial red flag. Operating cash flow was negative Rs 26.10 lakh in FY24, positive Rs 3.09 lakh in FY25 and negative Rs 67.79 lakh in FY26. Over those three years cumulative PAT was about Rs 9.2 crore (S18, S17). In FY26 inventory absorbed Rs 2.74 crore, receivables Rs 1.86 crore, a fall in payables Rs 1.15 crore, and taxes Rs 1.83 crore (S18). Inventory turnover slowed from 11.12x to 4.70x (S18).

blocks.caption: Profit vs operating cash flow (Rs crore) (S18, S17)

blocks.text: In three years the business has turned essentially none of its reported profit into operating cash, and management projects inventory rising further, to Rs 17.68 crore in FY27 (S20). Inventory building up much faster than sales in a fashion-sensitive product carries a risk of obsolescence and later write-downs.

Does the trend support the growth story? Partly. Revenue and margins have clearly improved. But the growth has been bought with working capital, and the IPO plan puts even more capital into inventory and showrooms. That will only pay off if B2C sell-through is much faster than the wholesale history suggests (S19, S20).

sections.title: Issue details and objects of the issue

blocks.text: This is a book-built NSE SME (Emerge) issue of 42,67,200 equity shares of Rs 10 face value at Rs 77-82, worth Rs 34.99 crore at the top of the band. It is entirely a fresh issue with no offer for sale (S1, S3). Of these, 2,14,400 shares are reserved for the market maker, Anant Securities, leaving a net issue of 40,52,800 shares (about Rs 33 crore) (S1, S13). The lot size is 1,600 shares, and individual investors must apply for at least 2 lots, which is Rs 2,62,400 at the upper price (S1).

blocks.caption: Issue at a glance (S1, S26)
rows: Opens 5 Oct 2026, closes 7 Oct 2026; allotment 8 Oct; listing 12 Oct (NSE SME)
Affinity Global Capital Market Pvt Ltd / Cameo Corporate Services Ltd

blocks.text: Some aggregators show a different reservation split (e.g., a 50% QIB quota, or a 3,200-share lot). The table above follows Chittorgarh's category-wise breakdown, which adds up to the full 42,67,200 shares (S26, S4).

Because the issue is all fresh, all the proceeds reach the company. Five named objects add up to Rs 24.06 crore, of which Rs 22.25 crore is for the plating facility, showrooms and their opening inventory (S20, S17). The remaining roughly Rs 10.93 crore of the Rs 34.99 crore gross would go to general corporate purposes and issue expenses. Upstox gives the split as about 63.5% capex, 31.2% general corporate purposes and 5.1% working capital (S12). The exact rupee split between GCP and issue expenses could not be confirmed from the sources reviewed.

blocks.text: Data conflict: Chittorgarh lists working capital at Rs 5.21 crore and net proceeds at Rs 27.47 crore (S1). Five other sources, including the DRHP-based Multibagg summaries, give Rs 1.81 crore for working capital (S17, S19, S3, S4). The Rs 1.81 crore figure is used here. The RHP may have revised it, and that could not be checked directly.

subsections.title: What the money actually buys and execution status

blocks.text: The total capex programme is Rs 27.55 crore, with Rs 5.30 crore to come from internal sources (S20). Given negative operating cash flow, that internal funding, plus the Rs 10.53 crore of FY27 working capital also meant to come from internal sources, is a stretch (S18, S19).

items: Plating facility: building-plan approvals were targeted for September 2026, construction runs to June 2027, testing in July-August 2027, and handover in September 2027. The trade licence, factory registration, consents to establish and operate, and fire licence are all still pending (S20).
Showrooms: completion is targeted for February 2027. The Ezra Street premises are held only under an MoU, with trade, fire and shop-establishment licences pending (S20).
Strategic logic: bring plating in-house to cut transit delays to Mumbai subcontractors, and move toward B2C for faster cash realisation, at the cost of carrying more inventory (S20).
None of the proceeds go to debt repayment or to promoters (S1, S3).

blocks.text: This is a single-family business. MD Qasim (Md. Kasim), about 70, is founder, Chairman and Managing Director with 12+ years in the industry, and oversees procurement, suppliers and quality. His three sons are also promoters and executive directors. Mohammed Usman, about 42, a commerce graduate, is Director and CEO and runs overall operations. Mohammed Imran, about 35, a commerce graduate, is Whole-time Director in charge of customers and distribution, with 9 years in jewellery. MD Aurangzeb, about 39, a commerce graduate, is Director in charge of marketing and brand, and took City Girl onto digital platforms (S9, S22).

blocks.caption: Pre-offer shareholding (S22)
rows: Promoter group (Shaista Usman, Afreen Imran, Farah Aurangzeb)

blocks.text: Pay is modest: Rs 9.60 lakh a year for the CEO and Rs 1.8-3 lakh for the others (S22). There is no holding company, subsidiary, associate or JV (S22). No other promoter ventures are disclosed in the sources reviewed. The promoters' experience is entirely in regional jewellery trading. None has disclosed experience running a manufacturing plant (like the planned plating facility) or a multi-floor retail format.

subsections.title: Board, related-party transactions and capital history

blocks.text: The seven-member board has four family executives and three independent directors: Sayak Dutta (FCA, audit committee chair), Babita Singh and Soumi Mitra (FCA). All three independents were appointed on 25 February 2026, about three months before the DRHP was filed (S22). That is common for SME IPOs, but it means board oversight has no track record.

Related-party transactions were Rs 8.82 crore (66.40% of revenue from operations) in FY24, Rs 1.08 crore (6.10%) in FY25 and Rs 3.28 crore (10.79%) in FY26 (S17). The sources reviewed do not name the counterparties or the type of transaction. The very high FY24 share coincides with a March 2024 amalgamation scheme (S23), which suggests group-entity trading was folded into the company. That link is an inference and has not been confirmed. The FY26 level of about 11% of revenue is still above what is typical and is worth watching.

items: A 16:1 bonus on 19 March 2026 took the share count from 6,61,739 to 1,12,49,563 shares. Promoters' average acquisition cost is Rs 0.37 per share (Usman) and Rs 0.65 per share (Qasim) (S23).
In May 2025 a loan was converted into 2,223 shares at Rs 272 per share (pre-bonus) (S23).
There are no rent agreements for the registered office or main business premises, which the company attributes to the 2018 fire (S24).

blocks.text: Litigation is minor. Three income-tax demands total Rs 33.23 lakh: Rs 32.03 lakh for AY2018-19, including about Rs 8.6 lakh of accrued interest, and Rs 1.19 lakh for AY2019-20. TDS defaults total Rs 800, and there is a Rs 2,875 personal tax demand on one officer (S25). There are no criminal cases, no regulatory actions, no GST proceedings and no SEBI or exchange penalties (S25). The prospectus does not say whether the AY2018-19 demands were paid or contested (S25). Relative to net worth of about Rs 18 crore this is small.

Lock-in: the minimum promoter contribution of 20% of post-issue capital is locked in for three years from allotment. Promoter holdings above that are subject to one-year and two-year lock-ins as disclosed (search-result summary of the offer document) (S29). That is a shorter release schedule than on the mainboard. As the bonus shares came in 2026, most of the promoters' 72.26% post-issue stake could become tradable within one to two years.

Overall, governance is routine for a family SME and there is no evidence of misconduct. The concerns are structural rather than accusatory: complete family control, independents appointed just before the IPO, a high related-party share in FY24, and missing lease paperwork.

items: Cash conversion and inventory: operating cash flow was negative in two of the last three years despite rising profits. Inventory days rose from 38 to 117 and are projected at 144, which risks stale stock in a trend-driven product (S18, S19).

Execution risk on objects: the plating plant has no signed machinery agreements and all its approvals are pending, with handover not due until September 2027. Ezra Street is held only under an MoU. Delays would leave money unused or push costs up (S20).

Pivot to B2C retail: the company is moving from 82.53% wholesale into multi-floor showrooms that need Rs 5.60 crore of opening inventory, a different skill set from the wholesale relationships that drive current revenue (S21, S20).
Geographic concentration: 86.32% of revenue comes from four eastern states and 65.77% from West Bengal alone, and the share has been rising (S8).

Dependence on outsourced labour and suppliers: production relies on non-exclusive karigars and contract manufacturers, the top 10 suppliers are 45.85% of purchases, and Maharashtra supplies 48.60% of raw materials (S2, S21).
Sustainability of margins: FY24 operating EBITDA was about Rs 0.11 crore. The 20%+ PAT margin is a one-year phenomenon, helped by Rs 1.18 crore of other income (S1, S17).

Governance and premises: complete family control (99.67% pre-issue), related-party transactions of 66.40% of revenue in FY24 and 10.79% in FY26, and no lease documents for the core Bagree Market premises (S22, S17, S24).
SME liquidity: a Rs 2.62 lakh minimum ticket, a single market maker, and promoter shares above the 20% minimum contribution unlocking within one to two years (S1, S29).

blocks.text: The first two risks, cash conversion and execution, carry the most weight. Together they decide whether the IPO money creates value or simply funds more inventory.

Customer concentration is low (top 5 at 11.11% of sales) even though it appears in the risk factors (S14). The tax litigation of Rs 33.24 lakh is small against net worth (S25). Debt is minimal (S1). E-commerce return fraud is listed as a risk, but online is under 5% of revenue (S14, S21). These are boilerplate-level risks for this company.

The lead manager, Affinity Global Capital Market, has a mixed record. A lead-manager tracker (search-result summary) shows 10 listed IPOs with an average listing gain of about 4%, of which 4 listed with gains and 6 with losses (S28). That is not a business risk, but it means the issue does not come with a strong distribution franchise behind it.

The only concrete forward-looking statements are the board-approved working-capital projections and the objects timeline in the offer document. Net working capital is projected to rise from Rs 7.48 crore (FY26) to Rs 12.34 crore (FY27) and Rs 18.79 crore (FY28), and inventory from Rs 7.82 crore to Rs 17.68 crore in FY27, to stock the new showrooms (S19, S20). The plating facility is targeted for handover in September 2027 and the showrooms for completion by February 2027 (S20).

Management's stated aims are to bring plating in-house to remove transit delays to Mumbai processors and speed up conversion of work in progress, and to shift toward B2C to get paid faster (S20). No revenue or margin guidance, investor call or interview with concrete targets was found. The sources reviewed contain no management statement on FY27 revenue growth.

Implied but not stated: an inventory projection of Rs 17.68 crore at 144 days implies management expects much higher FY27 sales volumes. Management has not put a revenue number on this, so investors should not infer one.

The plan is sensible in principle. Owning plating and running a flagship retail presence in Kolkata could improve margins and brand recall. But the projections assume the working-capital cycle stretches further, to 107 days, not that it improves (S19). The most important near-term signals are the Q1 FY27 run-rate (Rs 7.49 crore total income and Rs 1.83 crore PAT in one quarter) and whether H1 FY27 operating cash flow turns positive (S1, S18).

subsections.title: Day-1 status, anchors and grey market

blocks.text: This report was written on the opening day, 5 October 2026. On the opening morning no subscription data was available: Chittorgarh's subscription page said the information was 'not available at this time', and other trackers showed no category figures (S26, S16, S15, S5). Any day-1 numbers released later will be partial and say little about final demand. No anchor investor allocation is reported, and the QIB portion is only 43,200 shares (1.01%) (S26).

blocks.caption: Category allocation and status at time of writing (S26)

blocks.text: Grey market premium (unofficial, not an investment signal): Investorgain reported a GMP of Rs 0 on 3 October and again at 5:55 AM on 5 October 2026, that is, flat to the Rs 82 upper band, and noted that grey-market activity had barely begun (S11, S16). GMPs are unregulated and unreliable, and play no part in the verdict above.

method: Researched on 2026-10-05 (opening day) with WebSearch and WebFetch. MATERIAL GAP: I found the primary offer documents but could not read them directly. The DRHP on NSE archives (nsearchives.nseindia.com/emerge/corporates/content/Registration_27052026221452_DRHP.pdf) timed out on three fetch attempts, the RHP on the lead manager's site (affinityglobalcap.in/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/RHP_LFINAL-1.pdf) was larger than the fetch tool's 10 MB limit, and a direct download was not permitted in this environment. So no figure here comes from my own reading of the prospectus. Instead I relied on a series of nine DRHP-based articles by Multibagg (S2, S8, S17-S25), which quote DRHP figures to the lakh, and cross-checked the headline numbers (revenue, PAT, net worth, borrowings, objects, shareholding, geographic mix, cash flow) against at least two other aggregators (Chittorgarh, Groww, Upstox, Chanakya Nipothi, IPO Watch, Kotak Neo, Anand Rathi, DSIJ, Business Remedies). Discrepancies and how I resolved them: (1) EBITDA appears as 7.34/2.98/0.11 crore in some sources and 8.52/3.03/1.29 crore in others. The gap equals other income exactly, so both are shown.
